An equal or older version never wins, whatever order the files arrive in. Next, a look inside the Delta table, at how it remembers every one of these merges.

A Delta table is not one file. It is a folder of Parquet data files and, beside them, a folder called underscore delta log, and that log is what makes it a table. The terminal on the right lists it for Silver: one numbered JSON file per commit, from zero to four, each with a checksum beside it. The left of the frame draws them as a chain. Version zero wrote the empty table. Version one is the merge of batch forty one, four hundred rows inserted. Version two, batch forty two: eighteen inserted, one hundred and two updated. Version three, the correction file: three updated. Version four, the replay: nothing inserted, nothing updated. The file history dot p y reads that same log through Delta's own history call, and the numbers are the ones the merge printed, because they come from the commits themselves. Then it does something a plain folder of files cannot: it reads the table as of version one, before batch forty two ever arrived. The answer is drawn below the chain: L C twenty forty one at version one, two million. Nothing was copied to keep that answer; the old data files were simply never deleted, and the log knows which ones made up version one. This is how a question about last night's numbers can be answered after tonight's run. Next, the other tables Silver needs: the risk team's reference data.

Silver now knows every letter of credit, and which counterparty applied for each. Exposure is reported by counterparty group, against each group's limit, and both of those come from the risk team, as the two files landed in the reference container in Course five. The new file, reference tables dot p y, reads both files for one business date and, before anything else, checks them. There are five checks, drawn in the side pane: every counterparty I D appears once; every counterparty has a group; there is one limit per group and currency; every limit is a positive amount; and every group that has a limit is also in the mapping. The highlighted lines are the point of the file: if any check fails, nothing is published, and Silver keeps the reference tables it already had. The reason is in the note. A wrong mapping does not break anything visibly. It moves money from one group to another, and the morning report would show a group under its limit that is really over it. Only when all five pass does the script write both tables to Silver, in Delta, with the limit cast to decimal eighteen two. The terminal shows all five passing, and the result: eleven mappings and five limits, as of the thirty first of October. Next, the gate that checks Silver as a whole, before Gold may run.

The third gate, G three, sits between Silver and Gold. G two checked rows one by one; G three checks Silver as a whole, and the reference tables against it. The new function is in gates dot p y, and it runs three checks, drawn in the side pane. First, every L C I D appears once in Silver, which the merge should guarantee. Second, every open letter of credit, issued, active or amended, has a counterparty the mapping knows. Third, every group and currency with open exposure has a limit. The second check is the highlighted join: a left anti join, which keeps the open letters of credit that found no group. The terminal shows the run. One row per L C: pass, none duplicated. Every group and currency limited: pass. But every open L C mapped: fail, and the gate prints exactly which. One letter of credit, L C twenty two ninety nine, one point two million dollars, open, applied for by counterparty C P fifteen oh one, which is not in the risk team's mapping. The side pane follows it from the letter of credit to the missing group, and to the result: G three fails, and Gold does not run tonight. That might look harsh for one letter of credit out of four hundred and eighteen. Next, what would have happened if the gate were not there.

To see why G three refuses to let Gold run, take the gate away. Joins dot p y sums the open amount per currency in two ways, and the only difference between them is one word, highlighted in the editor. Both start from the same open letters of credit and join them to the counterparty mapping, to find each one's group. One uses a left join, which keeps every letter of credit, even when no group is found, and leaves the group empty. The other uses an inner join, which keeps only the letters of credit that found a group, and drops the rest without a message. The side pane draws the two paths. The terminal shows Spark's own table, and the side pane repeats it. In euros, both joins agree: six point five two million. In dollars, the left join finds twenty two point one two five million, and the inner join twenty point nine two five million. One point two million dollars is gone: L C twenty two ninety nine, the letter of credit G three named. There was no error and no warning. The total is just smaller, and a smaller exposure is the dangerous direction: a group would look further from its limit than it is. An inner join is the natural thing to write, which is exactly why a gate must check the reference data before Gold runs. Next course, Gold itself, and the answer the desk is waiting for.

Gold is where the desk's question gets its answer: how much could Syndica Bank still have to pay, for each counterparty group, against its limit. G three failed in the last section, and in Course eleven that failure will stop the nightly run. Here, the pipeline is built one piece at a time, so Gold is written against Silver as it stands, and the unmapped letter of credit simply has no group yet. The first piece is the rule, and it is a business rule, not a technical one. A letter of credit that is issued, active or amended is still open: the bank may still have to pay, so its exposure is its full amount. One that is cancelled, closed or expired can no longer be drawn, so its exposure is zero. The function exposure, at the top of the new gold dot p y, says exactly that, in the two highlighted lines. The terminal counts Silver's letters of credit by status and shows which ones count. The side pane groups them. One hundred and sixteen are open: thirteen active, seventy nine amended, twenty four issued. Three hundred and two are closed. Notice what the rule does not do. A closed letter of credit keeps its amount in Silver; only its exposure is zero. Gold derives a new column, and never edits a fact. Next, the table that every number in Gold is summed from.

Every report the desk reads will be a sum, and a sum is only as trustworthy as the rows beneath it. So Gold's first table is the fact table, fact L C exposure, at the finest grain there is: one row per letter of credit. The side pane draws how it is built. It starts from Silver's current rows, applies the exposure rule, and then joins the counterparty mapping, to give each letter of credit its group. That join, highlighted in the editor, is a left join, for the reason the last course found: an inner join would silently drop the letter of credit with no group, and its money with it. With a left join it keeps its row, with an empty group, where G three, and anyone reading the table, can see it. The terminal shows four hundred and eighteen rows, one per letter of credit, the same count as Silver. Then fact dot p y lists one group's open letters of credit: Woodgrove has three, all in dollars, from three of its companies. Two point two million amended, the one followed since Course five, five million active, and two point five million issued. Together, nine point seven million dollars. That is the number the morning report will carry for Woodgrove, and from here on every figure in Gold can be traced back to rows like these. Next, adding them up, without adding up what must never be added.

The aggregate table, agg group exposure, sums the fact table into one row per group. Except that is not quite right, and the highlighted line in the editor says why: it groups by group name and currency. Contoso has letters of credit in euros and in dollars, so Contoso gets two rows. The side pane draws them: three point one million euros, and four point eight five million dollars. The tempting thing is to add them and report one figure for Contoso, and there is no correct way to do it. Adding them as they stand mixes two units. Converting first needs an exchange rate, and a rate is a market price at a moment, not something the desk's limits were set in. This repository holds to that as an invariant: amounts in different currencies are never summed. The terminal shows the whole aggregate: Contoso in both currencies, Fabrikam three point four two million euros, Northwind six point three seven five million dollars, and Woodgrove nine point seven million dollars, the same figure the fact rows added up to. The aggregate keeps only rows with a group, so the unmapped letter of credit is not in any of them; G three is what keeps that from passing quietly. And the risk team's limits are set per currency too, so each of these rows will be compared with its own limit. Before that, a word about the type these amounts are kept in.

Every amount in this pipeline has been decimal eighteen two since Silver, and the new file, money dot p y, shows why, in Spark's own arithmetic. It asks Spark S Q L for one sum, twice: zero point one plus zero point two, first as doubles, the ordinary floating point numbers, then as decimals with two places. The terminal shows the answer, and the side pane draws it. As a double, the sum is zero point three, followed by fifteen zeros and a four. Neither zero point one nor zero point two can be written exactly in binary, so each is stored as the nearest value it can hold, and the small errors add up. As a decimal, the answer is zero point three zero, exactly, every time, because a decimal counts whole cents. One sum is off by a tiny amount. Summed over hundreds of letters of credit, those amounts drift by cents, and a total that should equal a limit can land a cent either side of it: two runs could disagree about a breach. So the side pane follows the type from end to end. TradeBook stores numeric eighteen two. Bronze keeps the amount as the string it arrived as, so nothing is converted on the way in. Silver casts it to decimal eighteen two, and the last line of the terminal reads the type straight from the fact table's schema: decimal eighteen two. Next, the numbers the desk actually reads: each group against its limit.

An exposure figure means little on its own. The desk needs to know how close each group is to the limit the risk team set. Gold dot p y now joins each row of the aggregate to its limit, on group and currency together, and derives three columns, highlighted in the editor and written out in the side pane. Utilisation is exposure as a percentage of the limit. Headroom is the limit minus the exposure: how much more the desk could issue. And breach is yes when the headroom falls below zero. The terminal shows Spark's table, and the side pane draws each group against its own limit. Contoso is at seventy seven point five percent in euros, and eighty point eight in dollars. Northwind, seventy nine point seven percent. Woodgrove, ninety seven percent. And Fabrikam's euro exposure is three point four two million against a limit of three million: one hundred and fourteen percent, in breach. That line is why the report exists. A breach is not a data error and Gold does not hide it or stop for it; it is the business news the desk must act on, this morning. Everything before this point existed so that this one yes can be believed. One question remains before Gold is published: how would anyone know if Gold itself were wrong? Next, the last gate.

Gold has two tables, and they describe the same money two ways: the fact table, one row per letter of credit, and the aggregate, one row per group and currency. Per currency, the two totals must be equal, to the cent. That is the fourth gate, G four, the function in the editor: it sums the fact's mapped exposure per currency, sums the aggregate per currency, and compares them. To see it work, this step plants a bug, of a kind that is easy to write. Someone filters the aggregate to letters of credit that are still open, and writes open as issued or active, forgetting amended. The side pane shows the line. The terminal shows the result, and nothing about it looks broken: every group gets a number, and no group is in breach. Woodgrove reads seventy five percent. That is the danger. Then G four runs. In euros, the fact says six point five two million and the aggregate one point five two one million. In dollars, twenty point nine two five million against ten point zero zero nine million. Fail, and Gold is not published. Every amended letter of credit, seventy nine of them, fell out of the aggregate, and no other check would have noticed, because a smaller exposure raises no alarm. Next, the bug removed, and the answer the desk has been waiting for.

The planted filter is gone from gold dot p y, and the run is repeated. The terminal shows G four on the fixed Gold: the fact and the aggregate agree in both currencies, and Gold is published. Then the last file of the course, answer dot p y, reads one row of the published aggregate and prints it the way the desk asked for it, for Woodgrove, in dollars. The side pane draws it as the summary card. Gross exposure: nine point seven million dollars. Limit: ten million dollars. Utilisation: ninety seven percent. Headroom: three hundred thousand dollars. Breach: no. Behind each of those numbers is the whole pipeline. The rows were extracted from TradeBook and checked at landing by G one. Bronze kept every delivery, and G two set aside what could not be trusted. Silver kept one true row per letter of credit, ignored the late older version, and G three checked it against the reference data. Gold applied the exposure rule in decimal money, per currency, and G four proved its two tables agree. Woodgrove is not in breach, but it is close: one more letter of credit above the headroom would put it over. So far, all of this has been run by hand, one command at a time. Next course, it runs every night, by itself, and we see what happens on the night it fails.

Course eleven's run dot p y runs the night as one program: Bronze, Silver, G three, Gold, G four, stopping at a failed gate. On Databricks, the same night is a job, and this section declares it in Terraform, validated, as the label says. A job is a set of tasks with dependencies, run on a cluster the job starts for itself and stops when it is done. The editor shows the shape. The task list, highlighted, is the same five steps, in order; G two runs inside the Bronze task. Each task depends on the one before it, which is the other highlighted line: the first task depends on nothing, and every other on its predecessor. The side pane draws the result as the graph Databricks would show. That dependency is the gate policy in the job's own terms. G three's task exits with an error when a check fails, so the task fails, and a task whose dependency failed never starts. Gold is not built, and G four does not run, exactly as on Ana's laptop. The tasks run the project's own files, fetched from its Git repository at the start of each run, so what runs is what was reviewed. The cluster is described rather than kept: one worker, started per run, and gone when the night is over, so nothing is left running to pay for. The terminal shows the configuration validated. Next, the gate policy itself, run for real.

Every gate so far has been run by hand, and Ana has read its result and decided what to do. A nightly run has nobody to decide, so the decision has to be written down. That is the gate policy, and it has three outcomes, drawn at the top of the side pane. A pass, and the run goes on. A warning, and the run goes on, and says so: two quarantined rows are worth someone's attention in the morning, but they are not a reason to withhold the report. A fail stops every step after it. The new file, run dot p y, is one whole night: Bronze, then G two, then Silver, then G three, then Gold, then G four. The highlighted lines are the policy in code: when G three fails, the run exits, and Gold is never written. The terminal shows tonight's run, and the side pane follows it down. No new batch has arrived, so Bronze takes nothing. G two warns, two rows in quarantine. Silver merges. G three fails, on the same unmapped counterparty, C P fifteen oh one. And Gold does not run; it keeps the last good answer. That last part matters. A failed night does not leave the desk with no report, or with a wrong one. It leaves yesterday's answer in place, clearly yesterday's, until the mapping is fixed. Next, writing every one of these results down, where it can be queried.

Printing a gate's result to a terminal is fine while someone is watching. At two in the morning nobody is, and a week later someone will ask: when did this counterparty first fail to map, and did any night pass with it missing? So every gate writes its results to a table. Run dot p y now takes a run I D, and the highlighted lines turn each check into a row: the run, the gate, the rule, its status, and the detail. The rows are appended to the audit table, gate results, and never overwritten, so the table is the history of every night. On Azure it will be risk dot audit dot gate results, in the catalog; here it is a local Delta table. The side pane draws the flow, from the gates to one row per check, into the table, and to the question it answers. The terminal shows tonight's run again, under the run I D night forty four, failing at G three exactly as before. Then audit dot p y reads the table back, and the side pane shows its rows. The warning from G two, two rows quarantined. The failed G three check, every open L C's counterparty mapped. And the two G three checks that passed, because a pass is evidence too: it shows the check ran. With this table, what failed and when is a query, not a search through logs, and Course twelve will put an alert on it. The rest of this course runs on Azure: the job, the email, and the parent pipeline that runs it all.

A nightly job that fails quietly is worse than one that does not run at all: the desk would read yesterday's answer and not know it. So a failed night must tell someone. The editor shows the smallest version of that, in the job's Terraform, validated, as the label says: email notifications, on failure, to the risk engineers' shared address. The side pane follows a failed night through it. The G three task exits with an error. The jobs service marks the run failed, and sends the email, with the run, the task that failed, and a link to its output. The email says that something failed. It does not say why, and that is deliberate: the why is in the audit table from section three, where every check of every gate is a row with its detail. The engineer who reads the email at eight in the morning goes to the table and finds, in one query, that counterparty C P fifteen oh one has no group. Two channels, two jobs: one wakes someone up, the other tells them what to do. The terminal shows the configuration validated. Course twelve adds a third channel, an alert on the factory's own logs, so that a failure that never reaches the job, such as the runtime being down, is noticed too. Next, the parent pipeline that ties the extract and the job together.

The night has two halves. Data Factory extracts, in the bank's network, through the runtime from Course seven. Databricks transforms, in the lake. Something has to run them in order, and only run the second when the first succeeded. That something is a parent pipeline in Data Factory, and the editor shows it: p l nightly, validated with the rest of the lab, as the label says. Its first activity, highlighted, executes Course seven's extract pipeline and waits for it to finish, so the batch is copied, checked by G one, sealed, and the watermark moved, before anything else happens. Its second activity, also highlighted, runs the Databricks job, and it depends on the first succeeding: if G one fails, the job never starts, and Bronze never sees a half delivered batch. The job is reached through a linked service that signs in as the factory's own identity, so once again there is no token or key anywhere. The side pane draws the chain from the trigger down. The tumbling window trigger from Course seven now starts p l nightly instead of the extract alone, passing it the window, the batch number, and the job's identifier, which Terraform fills in from the job it created. Inside the job, G two to G four decide whether Gold is published. The terminal shows the configuration validated. Next, why only one of the two services may own the schedule.

Both Data Factory and Databricks can run things on a schedule, and that is a trap. The side pane draws it on the left. Data Factory's trigger fires at two in the morning and, after the extract, starts the job. If the job also has its own schedule, say half past two, it starts itself as well, whether the extract has finished, succeeded or even run. On a slow night it reads a batch that has not landed; on a normal night, the night simply runs twice, and two runs merge and publish at once. The fix is to give the night one owner, drawn on the right. Data Factory's trigger is the only clock. The job runs only when the parent pipeline starts it, and so always after the extract, in order, once. The editor shows how that is written down, in the job's Terraform, validated, as the label says. The job still has a schedule, but its pause status is paused, highlighted. Declaring it paused, instead of leaving it out, is deliberate. A schedule left out can be added by anyone in the Databricks interface, and then nothing in the code says it should not be there. A schedule declared paused is visible in review, and the next apply sets it back to paused if someone switches it on. The terminal shows the configuration validated. Next, a night that fails, and how it is fixed.

This is what a failed night looks like from start to finish, run locally, with open-source Spark standing in for the Databricks job, as the label says. Night forty five runs, and G three fails, as it has every night since Course nine: one open letter of credit, L C twenty two ninety nine, belongs to counterparty C P fifteen oh one, which the risk team's mapping does not know. Gold does not run, and the desk keeps the last good answer. The fix does not belong in the pipeline. Nobody edits a join, or guesses a group in code. It belongs at the source: the risk team decides which group the counterparty belongs to, and sends a corrected mapping. The editor shows the file that arrived in Ana's inbox, and its last line, highlighted: Tailspin Imports, mapped to Northwind. The terminal publishes it to the lake for the first of November, and the reference checks from Course nine run on it before anything else: all five pass, twelve mappings, five limits. Then the night is run again. G three now passes every check, Gold is built, G four agrees in both currencies, and Gold is published. The side pane follows the night down, and shows what changed for the desk. Northwind's dollar exposure now includes the one point two million that was missing, and its utilisation moves from seventy nine point seven to ninety four point seven percent: closer to its limit than anyone could see while the mapping was missing. That is why G three refused to publish. Next, three kinds of progress that make every rerun like this one safe.

A nightly pipeline will fail one night, somewhere in the middle, and the most useful property it can have is that the answer to a failure is simply: run it again. This pipeline has that property, and the frame shows why. Each stage remembers how far it got, and each remembers it differently. On the left is the extraction, which remembers a watermark: the end of the last window it landed and sealed. The terminal reads it: the first of November, two in the morning. The watermark only moves after G one has sealed a batch, so after a failure the next run asks TradeBook for the same rows again, and nothing is lost or skipped. In the middle is Bronze, which remembers which batches it has taken, like a checkpoint. Run again, it reports every batch already in Bronze and appends nothing. On the right is Silver, and Silver's memory is different again. It keeps a list of merged batches too, and the first run finds nothing new. But then the list is deleted, as if Silver had lost track completely, and every batch is merged again from the start. Four hundred, one hundred and twenty, three, and four hundred rows: nothing inserted, nothing updated, every row ignored. Silver's real progress is the business state itself. A row only changes when a newer source version arrives, so replaying old batches changes nothing. Three different memories, one result: after a failure at any point, the same rerun is safe. Next course, watching the pipeline, paying for it, and shipping it.

Data Factory keeps a record of every run it makes: each pipeline run, each activity in it, each trigger firing. On its own, it keeps them for a few weeks, in its own screens. To ask questions of them, and to alert on them, they need to go somewhere that can be queried, alongside every other service's logs. That place is a Log Analytics workspace, and this section adds one, in Terraform, validated, as the label says. The editor shows the two resources. The workspace, log tradefin dev, keeps thirty days. And a diagnostic setting on the factory, highlighted, says what to send and where: three categories, pipeline runs, activity runs and trigger runs, to the workspace, one table each. The side pane draws the flow, from the factory, through the diagnostic setting, into the workspace, and the table beneath it names the three tables that appear there: A D F pipeline run, A D F activity run, and A D F trigger run. Each row in the activity table is one activity in one run: its pipeline, its name, its status, and when it failed, its error. A diagnostic setting is a small resource with a large effect. Nothing about the pipelines changes, but from now on every night's work is recorded somewhere a query can reach, and that is what the next two sections use. Next, the query itself, in K Q L.

Log Analytics is queried in K Q L, the Kusto query language, and its shape is easy to read once you see it: a table at the top, then a pipeline of steps, each taking the rows from the line above. The editor shows the query this course keeps in its own file, and the side pane takes it apart line by line. It starts from the A D F activity run table: every activity in every run the factory has made. The highlighted line keeps only the failed ones. The next keeps four columns: when, which pipeline, which activity, and the error code. And the last puts the newest first. Read top to bottom, it says exactly what it does: last night's failed activities, newest first. The query is not run here, as the label says: it lives in a file in the project, and the next section's alert reads that same file, so the query an engineer runs by hand in the morning and the one that pages them at night can never drift apart. The terminal shows the lab printing the file after validating the Terraform that uses it. One thing this table does not hold is the gates' own verdicts. Those are rows in the audit table from Course eleven, with every check and its detail. This table holds what the factory saw: a copy that failed, a runtime that did not answer, a lookup that timed out. Next, turning the query into an alarm.

A query answers when someone asks. An alert asks on its own. This section turns the last section's query into one, in Terraform, validated, as the label says, and the side pane draws its three parts. The signal is the query: failed rows in the activity table, read from the same file. The rule decides how often to ask and what counts: every fifteen minutes, it looks back over the last hour, and if there is even one failed activity, it fires. Those three settings are highlighted in the editor. And the action is the action group from Course three, a g trade risk, the same one the budget already uses, which emails the risk team's shared address. Keeping the action group separate from the rule means the people to tell are written down once, and every alarm in the subscription points at them. The table at the bottom shows why this alarm is needed even though the Databricks job already sends an email when a night fails. The job's email covers a night that reached the job and failed a gate. This alert covers everything that never reached the job at all: the extract that timed out because the runtime was down, as in Course seven, or a copy that could not reach TradeBook. Between the two, a failed night is never silent. Next, where the money goes.

Every resource in this film has used something billable, and Azure records each use as a usage record: which resource, which product, how much. The Consumption A P I reads them, and the terminal does, filtered, as always, to this course's own resources. The first command counts the records by product, and the list is a fair summary of the whole film: private D N S and private link from Course six, the lake's storage, a little bandwidth between regions, the N A T gateway that gives the bank's network its way out, public addresses, and Key Vault. The second command shows one record in full, and the table in the side pane repeats it: a product, then a quantity and a cost, both reported as none. That is not a mistake in the query. This subscription is a free trial, and its offer reports what was used, but not what it cost, through this A P I. On a paid subscription the same records carry the price, and the same query, grouped by product, is the month's bill. Until then, the honest way to put numbers on it is the way Course two and Course eight did: Azure's own retail prices, multiplied by usage stated as assumptions. Either way, the lesson from Course two holds: you pay for what you leave running, which is why every course in this film ends with the subscription empty. Next, two environments from one module.

Everything so far has been built in one environment, dev. A bank will want a second, prod, and the risk is that the two drift apart, one hand edit at a time, until prod is something nobody can rebuild. With Terraform the answer is to write the infrastructure once and make the environment a parameter. The label says how far this section goes: the configuration is validated offline, which is real, but prod is not deployed, because prod belongs in its own subscription. The editor shows the one change to the code. The state backend no longer names its state file. The key now comes from a small file per environment, passed to terraform init. The terminal lists the environment folder: for each environment, a backend file naming its state blob, dev dot t f state or prod dot t f state, and a variables file setting env to dev or prod. Every resource name already includes the environment, so the same code makes r g tradefin dev in one and r g tradefin prod in the other. Then terraform validate: the configuration is valid. The side pane draws the shape. One root module, every resource written once. Two pairs of small files. Two state files, so that a plan for dev can never touch prod. And two subscriptions, each with its own access and its own bill. Promoting a change is then just applying the same commit to the other environment. Next, the last section: where this pipeline could go from here.

Everything in this film was applied by a person at a terminal. A bank wants changes applied by a pipeline instead, from reviewed code, the same way every time. The usual risk is the credential: a pipeline that deploys to Azure needs to sign in, and a password stored in the C I system can leak. This section removes it. The editor shows a GitHub Actions workflow, and the label is precise about what is real: the Azure side is validated in Terraform, and the workflow is shown, not run. Two lines are highlighted. The workflow asks GitHub for an identity token for this run, and the Azure login step exchanges that token, instead of a secret, for access. The side pane follows it. GitHub signs a short lived token that says which repository and which branch this run is from. Entra I D trusts that token through a federated credential, on a managed identity made for deployment, and only for this repository's main branch: a fork, another branch or another repository gets nothing. The identity is allowed to change this resource group, and nothing more. Then Terraform plans and applies, exactly as at the terminal. Nothing secret is stored in GitHub at all. The three identifiers it needs are variables, because an identifier says who, but proves nothing. Next, where this pipeline could go from here.
